title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) comparing a baseline LLM intent→configuration pipeline to a verifier‑augmented pipeline that applies a deterministic sandbox validator. Design: N=200 preregistered synthetic intent→configuration tasks in a paired design with two permitted generation semantics; the executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve model calls. Model: gpt-5-mini. Primary estimand: paired difference in unsafe‑proposal rates (guarded − baseline) tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed=1729). Result (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200; contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Interpretation: under the executed shared semantics and sampled prompts the run produced no discordant pairs and therefore was non‑informative for the preregistered causal hypothesis. We (1) publish the complete preregistered run and deterministic artifacts (archived bundle — see Disclosure), (2) give an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure (shared generation + zero baseline unsafe rate + no repairs invoked), and (3) provide concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory budget, deterministic pilot checks, and alternative estimands) to enable informative repeats.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to lower operator effort in network operations but carries acute operational risk: misordered or unsafe configuration changes can cause outages or security regressions. A widely advocated mitigation is tool‑augmentation — coupling generation with deterministic validators/sandboxed simulators in generate–validate–repair pipelines so that proposed changes are checked before execution. We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to test whether deterministic verifier augmentation reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM. The preregistration specified (i) a paired binary estimand (guarded − baseline SAFE rate), (ii) N=200 tasks produced by a deterministic generator, (iii) two permitted generation semantics (independent per‑arm vs shared_initial_candidate), (iv) a deterministic sandbox validator for post‑generation scoring, and (v) a power plan calibrated to detect an approximate 7 percentage‑point paired reduction under plausible baseline unsafe rates. The run executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve hosted model budget. Below we document the execution and analysis outputs, diagnose why the confirmatory test was non‑informative for the causal estimand, and give concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats.
sections.related_work: Contemporary surveys and prototype reports document rapid application of LLMs to NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis and limited remediation) while emphasizing safety and evaluation gaps (Bilal et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025/2026 surveys). Tool‑augmentation architectures (generate–validate–repair, divide–verify–refine) are repeatedly proposed and empirically shown to reduce constraint violations on curated tasks when the external verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints (Zhang et al.; Pan et al.; other recent method proposals). Practical literature on guardrails, schema‑based interfaces, and agent orchestration stresses trade‑offs: stricter guardrails reduce unsafe acceptances but can increase false refusals and operator burden unless ROC‑style diagnostics are measured (guardrail and red‑teaming reports). Methodological critiques further call for workflow‑centred, replayable, sandboxed evaluations with deterministic generators and archived validator traces rather than static QA metrics. Our run follows those desiderata (deterministic task generator, sandbox validator, preregistration, archived traces) and directly addresses a gap highlighted in the literature: reproducible, preregistered adversarial NetOps experiments that quantify the paired causal effect of adding a deterministic verifier under controlled generation semantics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand-2026-01-prereg-v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, operationalized as paired binary SAFE indicators from a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar (paired_binary_analysis_v1); paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Sampling and task generation. A deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and a limited field set (admin, mtu, vlan). Generator seeds were fixed; each task manifest included initial_state, an explicit required_sequence, and difficulty metadata. Tasks included a preregistered adversarial transform set intended to raise baseline unsafe rates for confirmatory power. Pipelines compared. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: validate the same candidate in a deterministic sandbox; repairs could be invoked per the preregistration but were not applied in confirmatory episodes. Generation semantics and budgeting. The preregistration allowed (A) independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task → ~400 calls) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (one call per task → ~200 calls). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve hosted model budget; executed model_calls_used = 200. Scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted deterministic valid flags and structured traces (validation_before/after, violation lists). Confirmatory binaries were derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis and handling. The analysis executed exactly as preregistered (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Missingness and exclusion rules from the preregistration were enforced (one automatic retry per failed model call; contamination or verifier nondeterminism would cause exclusion and replacement). All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied bundle (see Disclosure) for deterministic replay.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Provider audit confirmed 200 hosted model call events and no nondeterministic verifier behavior. Primary confirmatory statistics. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every confirmatory candidate as valid: baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200. Paired contingency counts: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Representative diagnostics. Scoring JSONs and validator traces show validation_before/after with violation_count = 0 and validator.valid = true in every confirmatory episode; repair_provider_trace fields are null, confirming no repairs were invoked. Missingness and contamination. analysis/missingness_summary shows complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes; contamination summary records no flagged episodes. Inferential consequence. Because McNemar relies on discordant pairs (n10 and n01), the absence of discordant outcomes renders the preregistered paired contrast mechanically non‑informative for verifier efficacy under the executed semantics. The observed ceiling outcome reflects the conjunction of (a) shared per‑pair generation semantics, (b) zero baseline unsafe detections on the sampled prompts for this model and task family, and (c) absence of repairs that could have induced guarded‑arm discordance.
sections.discussion: Root‑cause diagnosis (artifact‑grounded). The degenerate contingency (n11 = 200, no discordant pairs) follows directly from archived facts: the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate per task scored by both arms), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned valid = true for every sampled candidate, and repair traces are null (no repairs applied). These archived artifacts together made arm‑level disagreements impossible under the executed procedure, so the confirmatory estimand could not be evaluated. Implications for experimental design. A paired estimand attributing causal effect to a verifier requires per‑arm opportunities for differing candidate proposals (independent per‑arm draws) or a repair mechanism that deterministically alters guarded candidates. When budget constraints push shared generation, alternative estimands should be preregistered (absolute baseline unsafe rate estimation, refusal‑rate estimation if repairs are applied, or exploratory ROC estimation using reserved calibration items). Recommendations for informative repeats (concrete, archived): (1) use independent per‑arm generation for confirmatory paired contrasts (preregister and budget ≈400 model calls for N=200 paired tasks) unless repairs will deterministically change outputs; (2) consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (we reserved up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe rates align with power assumptions and then freeze those transforms in the preregistration; (3) perform a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout and abort the confirmatory run if the pilot yields ceiling/floor contingency counts, following preregistered contingency‑preserving paths; (4) if repairs are part of the guarded pipeline, archive and analyze repair_provider_trace artifacts to quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and potential new violations; (5) consider alternative, testable estimands under shared semantics (absolute baseline unsafe rate with CIs; refusal‑rate estimation). Threats to validity and generalization. The synthetic task family was intentionally narrow (admin/mtu/vlan fields, single‑AS topologies); the deterministic validator encodes a specific formalization of full_intent_constraint_validation for that family and ran deterministically in sandbox; zero unsafe detections here do not imply production safety across multi‑vendor, multi‑AS, or richer configuration spaces. Operational implications. Operators must weigh the resource cost of independent per‑arm generation or calibration (additional model calls) against the risk of proceeding with an untested confirmatory design; our artifacts make per‑task resource trade‑offs explicit and replayable. Reproducibility. All numeric summaries and contingency tables are identical to archived analysis artifacts (condition_summary and paired_contingency_table). Representative scoring JSONs and shared response files show the identical generated candidate for both arms and the validator traces that produced the degenerate contingency. The archived bundle permits deterministic replay of the same non‑informative outcome and should be consulted before changing preregistered choices.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory budget, deterministic pilot checks, and alternative estimands) for informative repeats. Practitioners attempting similar evaluations should align model‑call budgets with estimand testability and consume exploratory reserves to calibrate adversarial strength prior to confirmatory testing.

Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred before the lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
